title: What is an inner class, why is it used, and what are the four types (non-static member, static nested, local, anonymous)?
shortTitle: What is an inner class and what are the four types?

s1_definition.profdef: An inner class is a class declared inside another class. Java supports four forms: a non-static member class (also called an inner class in the strict sense) that holds an implicit reference to an instance of the enclosing class; a static nested class that belongs to the enclosing class but holds no outer instance reference; a local class declared inside a method; and an anonymous class, an unnamed class defined and instantiated in a single expression. They are used to logically group a helper that is only meaningful to the outer class, to improve encapsulation, and to give a callback access to the enclosing scope.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India branch as the outer class. A non-static member class is like a teller who works inside that specific branch and can see the branch's safe and records because he belongs to that branch instance. A static nested class is like a standardized form template kept in the branch filing system; it belongs to the branch organization but does not need any particular branch's safe to exist. A local class is like a temporary note a clerk scribbles while doing one specific task and throws away after. An anonymous class is like grabbing a passer-by to sign one single form on the spot without ever learning their name.
s1_definition.oneliner: An inner class is a class nested inside another, and the four kinds are non-static member, static nested, local, and anonymous, each differing in whether it holds an outer instance and how widely it is visible.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An inner class is a class declared inside another class. Java supports four forms: a non-static member class (also called an inner class in the strict sense) that holds an implicit reference to an instance of the enclosing class; a static nested class that belongs to the enclosing class but holds no outer instance reference; a local class declared inside a method; and an anonymous class, an unnamed class defined and instantiated in a single expression. They are used to logically group a helper that is only meaningful to the outer class, to improve encapsulation, and to give a callback access to the enclosing scope.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India branch as the outer class. A non-static member class is like a teller who works inside that specific branch and can see the branch's safe and records because he belongs to that branch instance. A static nested class is like a standardized form template kept in the branch filing system; it belongs to the branch organization but does not need any particular branch's safe to exist. A local class is like a temporary note a clerk scribbles while doing one specific task and throws away after. An anonymous class is like grabbing a passer-by to sign one single form on the spot without ever learning their name.

**One line to remember:** An inner class is a class nested inside another, and the four kinds are non-static member, static nested, local, and anonymous, each differing in whether it holds an outer instance and how widely it is visible.

sections.s2_technical:
A non-static member class is declared directly inside another class without the `static` keyword. It holds an implicit reference to the enclosing instance, which means it can read and use the outer object's fields and methods directly. You create it only through an outer instance, like `Bank.Teller t = bank.new Teller();`. Because it keeps a hidden pointer to the outer object, a long-lived non-static inner class can accidentally keep the whole outer object alive, which is a memory-leak trap in senior-level code.

A static nested class is declared with `static`. It belongs to the enclosing class as a namespace but does not hold any reference to an outer instance, so you create it like a normal class, `Bank.Statement s = new Bank.Statement();`. It can only touch the outer class's static members. This is the safest and most common form for helper types; for example, a `Bank.TransferResult` record that just carries data. A small banking usage is `static class TransferResult { final String id; final BigDecimal amount; }`.

A local class is declared inside a method body, so it is visible only within that method. It can capture the method's effectively final local variables. It is useful when you need a small helper that is used only inside one method and nowhere else. An anonymous class is declared and instantiated at the same time, usually to implement an interface or extend a class on the spot. A banking example is passing a one-off comparator or a callback: `transferService.onComplete(new TransferListener() { public void completed(String id) { log.info("done " + id); } });`. Anonymous classes also capture effectively final locals and, like member inner classes, hold a reference to the enclosing instance when non-static.

The reasons to use inner classes are encapsulation and locality. If a helper type has no meaning outside its enclosing class, nesting it keeps it private and signals that intent. Non-static inner and anonymous classes are especially handy for callbacks that need the enclosing object's state, such as event listeners. The senior guidance is to prefer static nested classes whenever the helper does not actually need the outer instance, because they avoid the hidden outer reference and the associated leak risk, and in modern code a lambda often replaces an anonymous class that implements a single-method interface.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's transfer engine needs to return a small result object that bundles a transfer id and the final balances. This type has no meaning outside the engine. This is exactly what a static nested class is for, because it groups the helper inside the engine without needing any particular engine instance and without a hidden outer reference.

Problem 2 — Each branch keeps an internal auditor that must read that branch's own ledger to verify totals. The auditor only makes sense attached to a specific branch instance. This is exactly what a non-static member class is for, because it holds an implicit reference to its enclosing branch and can read the branch's private ledger directly.

Problem 3 — When a transfer finishes, the caller wants to react once, right here, without writing a whole named listener class. This is exactly what an anonymous class (or a lambda) is for, and inside the verification method we also use a tiny local class to format a line only used in that method.

In the mini-project we build a `Branch` outer class with a non-static `LedgerAuditor` member class, a static nested `TransferResult`, a local class inside a verification method, and an anonymous `TransferListener`. The demo transfers between Rajesh and Priya, audits the branch, and fires the anonymous callback.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a `Branch` named Mumbai-Main holding Rajesh at 1,000,000 and Priya at 250,000, with a transfer of 50,000 from Rajesh to Priya.

Step 1: Main creates the Branch and registers both accounts into the branch's private ledger map. The data now lives inside the outer Branch instance.

Step 2: Main calls `transfer` and passes an anonymous `TransferListener`. The transfer debits Rajesh to 950,000 and credits Priya to 300,000, then invokes the anonymous class's completed method, which logs the callback using the captured transfer id and amount.

Step 3: The transfer method builds a static nested `TransferResult` holding the id and both final balances and returns it by value. Because TransferResult is static, it carries no reference back to the Branch.

Step 4: Main creates a non-static `LedgerAuditor` through the branch instance. Inside `verifyTotals`, a local class `LineFormatter` formats each line, and the auditor reads the enclosing branch's private ledger directly because it holds the implicit outer reference, summing to 1,250,000.

```text
[INFO] callback: transfer Mumbai-Main-TXF-1 of Rs.50000 done
[INFO] Result id=Mumbai-Main-TXF-1 rajesh=Rs.950000 priya=Rs.300000
[INFO] Branch Mumbai-Main total across ledger = Rs.1250000
```

```text
    │     debit SAV2001 → 950,000
    │     credit CUR3001 → 300,000

          verifyTotals()

            reads OUTER ledger directly → sum = 1,250,000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An inner class is simply a class declared inside another class, and Java gives me four distinct forms. The first is the non-static member class, which many people call the true inner class, and its defining feature is that it holds an implicit reference to an instance of the enclosing class, so it can read and use the outer object's fields and methods directly. Because you need an outer instance to create it, you write something like branch dot new LedgerAuditor. The second is the static nested class, declared with the static keyword, which belongs to the enclosing class as a namespace but holds no reference to any outer instance, so you create it like a normal class and it can only touch the outer class's static members.

The third form is the local class, declared inside a method body and visible only within that method, which can capture the method's effectively final local variables and is useful for a tiny helper used in exactly one place. The fourth is the anonymous class, which is declared and instantiated in a single expression, usually to implement an interface or extend a class on the spot, and it is perfect for one-off callbacks. In my banking transfer engine I used all four: a static nested TransferResult to carry the id and final balances back to the caller, a non-static LedgerAuditor that reads its branch's private ledger directly, a local class to format audit lines inside one method, and an anonymous listener fired when a transfer completes.

The reason I reach for inner classes is encapsulation and locality. When a helper type has no meaning outside its enclosing class, nesting it keeps it private and clearly signals that intent, and the non-static and anonymous forms are especially good for callbacks that need the enclosing object's state.

The senior nuance I always raise is two-fold. First, I prefer a static nested class whenever the helper does not actually need the outer instance, because a non-static inner class keeps a hidden reference to its enclosing object, and if that inner instance is long-lived, it can keep the entire outer object alive and cause a subtle memory leak. Second, in modern Java, an anonymous class that implements a single-method interface is almost always better written as a lambda, which is shorter and does not generate a separate class file. So my rule of thumb is: static nested by default, non-static only when you genuinely need the outer state, local for one-method helpers, and a lambda instead of an anonymous class wherever the target is a functional interface.

---

keyPoints: Member inner class: non-static, has access to outer instance
Static nested class: declared with static, no access to outer instance
Local class: defined inside a method, captures effectively final locals
Anonymous class: no name, inline implementation of interface or class
